s: Bahadur Shah I, who succeeded Aurangzeb, is also known by which epithet?

s:
Consider the following statements regarding Jahandar Shah:

2. He was supported by Wazir Zulfiqar Khan.
3. He ruled under the influence of Lal Kunwar.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Jahandar Shah was called Lampat, was backed by Zulfiqar Khan and remained under the sway of his mistress Lal Kunwar.

o: He was deposed and killed by Farrukh Siyar and the Sayyids.
He was exiled to Rangoon after the Revolt of 1857.
He was blinded and pensioned by the Company.
He died in office after appointing a successor.
x: Jahandar Shah was deposed and killed by Farrukh Siyar and the Sayyid brothers.
tq: Test the fate of a ruler through a person-and-event association.
sec: Later Mughals - chronological order, epithets and fate  [APPSC]

s: Farrukh Siyar issued the farman favourable to the English East India Company in which year?
x: Farrukh Siyar issued the important farman granting favourable trading privileges to the Company in 1717.
tq: Use numerical discrimination among closely spaced years in the Later Mughal period.
sec: Later Mughals - chronological order, epithets and fate  [APPSC]

s: Which of the following correctly describes the fate of Farrukh Siyar?
o: He was murdered by Imad-ul-Mulk in 1759.
He was blinded, deposed and killed by the Sayyids in 1719.
He died in office after releasing Shahu.
He was blinded by Ghulam Qadir Rohilla in 1788.
x: Farrukh Siyar was blinded, deposed and killed by the Sayyid brothers in 1719.
tq: Distinguish similar violent ends of different Later Mughal emperors.
sec: Later Mughals - chronological order, epithets and fate  [APPSC]

s: Who among the following was popularly known as ‘Rangeela’?
x: Muhammad Shah, who ruled from 1719 to 1748, was known as Rangeela.
tq: Directly identify the ruler associated with a well-known epithet.
sec: Later Mughals - chronological order, epithets and fate  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements about Muhammad Shah:
1. He got rid of the Sayyid brothers with the help of Nizam-ul-Mulk.
2. Nizam-ul-Mulk, Saadat Khan and Murshid Quli Khan became autonomous during his reign.
3. Nadir Shah invaded India during his reign.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All three statements are correct. Muhammad Shah eliminated the Sayyid influence with Nizam-ul-Mulk’s help, witnessed the autonomy of major provincial rulers and faced Nadir Shah’s invasion in 1739.
tq: Check a ruler’s reign through political, provincial and invasion-related facts.
sec: Later Mughals - chronological order, epithets and fate  [APPSC]

s: Which pair is correctly matched?
o: Shah Alam II — Murdered by Imad-ul-Mulk
Alamgir II — Exiled to Rangoon after 1857
Ahmad Shah — Blinded and deposed by Imad-ul-Mulk
Akbar II — Blinded by Ghulam Qadir Rohilla
x: Ahmad Shah was blinded and deposed by Imad-ul-Mulk. The other fates belong respectively to Bahadur Shah II, Alamgir II and Shah Alam II.
tq: Find the correctly matched ruler and fate among closely related Later Mughal events.
sec: Later Mughals - chronological order, epithets and fate  [APPSC]

s: Udham Bai, who exercised control during the reign of Ahmad Shah, bore which honorific title?
x: Udham Bai, who controlled affairs during Ahmad Shah’s reign, was honoured with the title Qibla-i-Alam.

sec: Later Mughals - chronological order, epithets and fate  [APPSC]

s: Which of the following developments took place during the reign of Alamgir II?
o: The Battle of Plassey was fought in 1757 and Abdali invasions continued.
Ram Mohan Roy received the title Raja.
The Third Battle of Panipat was fought and Buxar was won.
The Company granted pension to the first Mughal pensioner.
x: Repeated invasions by Ahmad Shah Abdali and the Battle of Plassey in 1757 occurred during Alamgir II’s reign.
tq: Associate events with the correct reign instead of relying only on chronology.
sec: Later Mughals - chronological order, epithets and fate  [APPSC]

s: With reference to Shah Alam II, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: He was the first Mughal ruler to release Shahu.
He became the first Mughal pensioner of the Company.
He was killed by the Sayyid brothers in 1719.
He gave Raja title to Ram Mohan Roy.
x: Shah Alam II became the first Mughal pensioner of the East India Company. He witnessed the Third Battle of Panipat and the Battle of Buxar during his reign.
tq: Separate the defining political position of Shah Alam II from facts belonging to other rulers.
sec: Later Mughals - chronological order, epithets and fate  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Bahadur Shah II — Exiled to Rangoon after 1857
Shah Alam II — Blinded by Ghulam Qadir Rohilla
Akbar II — Gave Ram Mohan Roy the title ‘Raja’
Muhammad Shah — Exiled to Rangoon after 1857
x: Muhammad Shah was not exiled to Rangoon. Bahadur Shah II was exiled to Rangoon after the Revolt of 1857; Shah Alam II was blinded by Ghulam Qadir Rohilla.
tq: Find the mismatched ruler and fate by eliminating well-known correct associations.
sec: Later Mughals - chronological order, epithets and fate  [APPSC]

s: Bahadur Shah II, also called Zafar, died in which year after his exile to Rangoon?
x: Bahadur Shah II was exiled to Rangoon after 1857 and died there in 1862.
tq: Distinguish the year of exile-related events from the year of death.
sec: Later Mughals - chronological order, epithets and fate  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Shah Alam II returned to Delhi under the protection of Mahadji Scindia.
2. He returned to Delhi in 1771–72.
3. Before returning, he lived at Allahabad under Company protection.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All three statements are correct. Shah Alam II lived at Allahabad under Company protection and returned to Delhi in 1771–72 under Mahadji Scindia’s protection.
tq: Test a sequence of political circumstances rather than a single isolated date.
sec: Later Mughals - chronological order, epithets and fate  [APPSC]

s: Murshid Quli Khan held which offices in Bengal?
x: Murshid Quli Khan first served as Diwan and later became Nazim of Bengal. He ruled Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?

Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk — Subedar of Awadh
Ali Muhammad Khan — Nawab of Carnatic under the Nizam
x: Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk became Subedar of Awadh in 1722 and founded the autonomous state of Awadh.

sec: Regional successor states → founder and position held; Sayyid brothers as king-makers  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Carnatic state:

3. Saadatullah Khan named his nephew Dost Ali as successor without the Nizam’s approval.

x: All three statements are correct. Saadatullah Khan founded the Carnatic or Arcot state and named Dost Ali, his nephew, as successor without the Nizam’s approval.

s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:

s: The Sayyid brothers who acted as king-makers during the period 1713–1720 were:
o: Abdullah Khan and Husain Ali Khan
Murshid Quli Khan and Ali Muhammad Khan
x: The Sayyid brothers were Abdullah Khan, who served as Wazir, and Husain Ali Khan, who served as Mir Bakhshi.

sec: Regional successor states → founder and position held; Sayyid brothers as king-makers  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following statements regarding the Sayyid brothers is NOT correct?
o: Husain Ali Khan was the Mir Bakhshi.
They were eliminated during the reign of Farrukh Siyar in 1713.
They dominated Mughal politics from 1713 to 1720.

s: Which of the following statements about the regional successor states is correct?
o: Nizam-ul-Mulk was initially the Subedar of the Deccan and later became Wazir.
Murshid Quli Khan founded Rohilkhand as an Afghan chief.
Muhammad Khan Bangash served as Subedar of Awadh in 1722.
Saadat Khan founded Bengal as its Diwan.
x: Nizam-ul-Mulk held the position of Subedar of the Deccan and later became Wazir. The other statements interchange the founders and offices of Bengal, Rohilkhand and Awadh.

s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Awadh succession:
1. Safdar Jung was the nephew and son-in-law of Saadat Khan.
2. Safdar Jung became Nawab of Awadh and Wazir.
3. Shuja-ud-Daula, who came later, fought at the Battle of Buxar.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All three statements are correct. Safdar Jung succeeded Saadat Khan in the specified family relationship and offices, and Shuja-ud-Daula later fought at Buxar.
tq: Test succession through relationship, office and a later military event.

s: Which of the following correctly describes the early development of Hyderabad?
o: It was first envisaged by Zulfiqar Khan, who governed through Daud Khan from 1708.
It was created by Ali Muhammad Khan during Abdali’s first raid.
It was founded by Murshid Quli Khan after the Battle of Buxar.
It was first envisaged by Saadat Khan as a province of Awadh.
x: Hyderabad was first envisaged by the Deccan viceroy Zulfiqar Khan, who governed through Daud Khan from 1708.
tq: Distinguish the initial conception of a state from the later founder traditionally associated with it.
sec: Regional successor states → founder and position held; Sayyid brothers as king-makers  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following statements about Nizam-ul-Mulk’s administration is correct?
o: He made Puran Chand his Diwan and followed a Mughal-type jagirdari administration.
He made Dost Ali his successor without the Nizam’s approval.
He governed Bengal through Murshid Quli Khan.
He abolished the jagirdari system and appointed Saadat Khan as Diwan.
x: Nizam-ul-Mulk was tolerant, appointed Puran Chand as his Diwan and administered Hyderabad through a Mughal-type jagirdari system.
tq: Apply administrative clues to identify the correct regional ruler.

s: Which one of the following correctly states the consequence of Ahmad Shah Abdali’s invasions?
o: Bengal and Bihar were ceded to him after the Battle of Karnal.
Punjab and Multan were ceded to him, and he repeatedly invaded during Alamgir II’s reign.
He established the autonomous state of Hyderabad with Puran Chand as Diwan.
He carried away the Peacock Throne after defeating Muhammad Shah at Karnal.
x: Punjab and Multan were ceded to Ahmad Shah Abdali, and his repeated invasions occurred during the reign of Alamgir II. The other options describe Nadir Shah’s actions or Hyderabad’s administration.

s:

Reason (R): They repeatedly challenged Mughal authority and drained the imperial treasury.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

s:
Consider the following statements regarding the establishment of the Asaf Jahi state:

2. He defeated Mubariz Khan at Shakar Kheda.
3. The independent Asaf Jahi state was established in 1748.

s: The Battle of Shakar Kheda, which enabled the establishment of the virtually independent Hyderabad state, was fought in:

s: Which one of the following statements about the first Nizam is correct?
o: He accepted the Subsidiary Alliance in 1798.
He kept the Marathas out of Hyderabad during his lifetime.
He was defeated at Shakar Kheda by Mubariz Khan.
x: The first Nizam kept the Marathas out during his lifetime. He died in 1748; the Subsidiary Alliance was accepted much later by Nizam Ali Khan.

s:
Arrange the following rulers of Hyderabad in chronological order of their accession:
A. Salabat Jung
B. Nasir Jung
C. Muzaffar Jung
D. Asaf Jah I
E. Nizam Ali Khan
Select the correct answer.
x: The order is Asaf Jah I (1724), Nasir Jung (1748), Muzaffar Jung (1750), Salabat Jung (1751), and Nizam Ali Khan (1762).
tq: Fix the first and last rulers, then arrange the closely spaced middle accessions.

s:

c. Afzal-ud-Daula
d. Mir Mahbub Ali Khan

List-II (Period of rule)

Mir Osman Ali Khan ruled from 1869 to 1911.
The dynasty continued as the ruling power after 1948.
Nizam Ali Khan was the last Nizam of Hyderabad.
x: Operation Polo integrated Hyderabad State into the Indian Union in 1948. Mir Osman Ali Khan was the last Nizam.
tq: Distinguish the end of the dynasty from the end of individual rulers.

x: Irfan Habib explained the decline through an agrarian crisis in The Agrarian System of Mughal India (1963), arguing that over-exploitation of peasants provoked revolts.

s: Which work is associated with Satish Chandra's explanation of the Mughal decline?
o: Parties and Politics at the Mughal Court, 1707–1740
x: Satish Chandra wrote Parties and Politics at the Mughal Court, 1707–1740 and associated decline with the jagirdari crisis.
tq: Use author–work discrimination among closely related historiographical titles.
sec: Historiography of decline → historian and book  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. M. Athar Ali — The Mughal Nobility under Aurangzeb
2. W. H. Moreland — India at the Death of Akbar
3. François Bernier — Travels in the Mogul Empire
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
x: All three pairs are correctly matched. Athar Ali examined the Mughal nobility, Moreland wrote India at the Death of Akbar, and Bernier wrote Travels in the Mogul Empire.
tq: Verify each author–work pair before selecting the combined code.
sec: Historiography of decline → historian and book  [APPSC]

s: M. Athar Ali attributed the worsening of the jagir shortage primarily to:
o: The transfer of all jagirs to European companies
The enlargement of the nobility through the inclusion of Deccanis and Marathas
The abolition of the mansabdari system by Farrukh Siyar
The decline of agriculture caused by Nadir Shah's raid
x: Athar Ali argued that the enlarged nobility, including Deccanis and Marathas, intensified the shortage of jagirs.
tq: Apply the historian's specific causal argument rather than choosing a general cause of decline.
sec: Historiography of decline → historian and book  [APPSC]

s: François Bernier's explanation of Mughal decline emphasised that:
o: The empire collapsed mainly because of the Maratha naval power.
The jagirdari crisis resulted from too few nobles in the imperial service.
The absence of private property in land reduced the incentive for improvement and led towards ruin.
Aurangzeb's religious policy alone caused the complete collapse of agriculture.
x: Bernier associated the absence of private property in land with a lack of incentive to improve it and predicted ruin.
tq: Identify the precise argument attached to the named historian.
sec: Historiography of decline → historian and book  [APPSC]

s: The revisionist interpretation of the eighteenth century views it chiefly as a period of:
o: Exclusive European control over the peasant surplus
Regional growth, with successor states controlling economic and law-and-order systems
Uninterrupted Mughal centralisation under weak successors
x: The revisionist view treats the eighteenth century as a period of regional growth. The new states managed their own economic and law-and-order systems and controlled peasant surplus.
tq: Contrast the revisionist regional-growth interpretation with the older collapse narrative.
sec: Historiography of decline → historian and book  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following was NOT a major cause of the decline of the Mughal Empire?
o: The invasions of Nadir Shah and Ahmad Shah Abdali
The long Deccan wars and the resulting drain on the treasury
The strengthening of central authority by independent nobles
x: Independent nobles weakened, rather than strengthened, central authority. The Deccan wars, Maratha rise and invasions were among the major causes of decline.
tq: Find the reversed effect in a cause-of-decline option.
sec: Causes of decline

s: At its greatest extent under Aurangzeb, the Mughal Empire extended approximately from:
o: Kashmir to Jinji and the Hindukush to Chittagong
Kabul to Bijapur and Sindh to Assam
Punjab to Madurai and the Arabian Sea to the Bay of Bengal
Delhi to the Narmada and Gujarat to Bengal
x: Under Aurangzeb the empire reached from Kashmir to Jinji and from the Hindukush to Chittagong.
tq: Recall both geographical limits together instead of relying on one directional clue.
sec: Causes of decline

s:
Consider the following statements about the causes of Mughal decline:
1. Aurangzeb's long Deccan wars weakened the foundations of the empire and drained the treasury.
2. The Sayyids' control contributed to corruption and mismanagement.
3. Peasant and zamindar revolts followed the jagirdari and agrarian crises.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All three statements are correct. Religious policies, prolonged warfare, factional noble politics, fiscal crisis and agrarian unrest combined to weaken the empire.
tq: Test cumulative causation by checking each internal cause separately.
sec: Causes of decline

s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched with a cause of Mughal decline?
o: European companies — a factor contributing to the decline
Noble rivalries — weakening of central authority
Maratha rise — restoration of Mughal authority
Agrarian crisis — shrinkage of the fiscal base
x: The Maratha rise weakened Mughal authority; it did not restore it. Noble rivalries, agrarian crisis and European companies were associated with the decline.
tq: Watch for the reversed consequence in a cause-and-effect pair.
sec: Causes of decline

s: The Farman of 1717 issued by Farrukh Siyar is significant because it:
o: Granted chauth and sardeshmukhi to Shahu's agent
Exempted the English Company from customs duties in Bengal
Granted the Company Diwani rights in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa
Transferred Kora and Allahabad to the Company

s: The Mughal grant of 1719, issued through the Sayyids, granted to Balaji Vishwanath, as Shahu's agent:

Kora and Allahabad with an annual payment
Chauth and sardeshmukhi of the six Deccan subas

Shah Alam II granted the Company the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.
Farrukh Siyar exempted the Company from customs duties in Bengal.

o: Regional states, the Marathas and finally the East India Company
The Rajputs, the Sikhs and the Portuguese
The Mughals, the Marathas and the Ottoman Empire
The Sayyids, the Afghans and the French alone

s: Which one of the following statements correctly distinguishes the raids of Nadir Shah and Ahmad Shah Abdali?
o: Nadir Shah took Punjab, whereas Abdali took the Koh-i-Noor and Peacock Throne.
Nadir Shah's raid occurred in 1739, while Abdali's raids began from 1748.
Nadir Shah's raids began in 1748, while Abdali invaded in 1739.
Both raids began in 1761 and ended with the Battle of Panipat.
x: Nadir Shah raided India in 1739, taking the Koh-i-Noor and Peacock Throne. Abdali's raids began from 1748, took Punjab and culminated in Panipat in 1761.
tq: Separate the two invaders by starting date and the distinctive result of each raid.
